item.title: Repairs to A15 motorway bridge will cost hauliers €600k a day
item.description:
Repairs to A15 motorway bridge will cost hauliers €600k a day

September 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The partial closure of a motorway bridge in Rotterdam for repairs is expected to cost the transport sector at least €600,000 a day because of longer journeys.

The bridge, which carries traffic on the A15 to the Maasvlakte, was closed a week ago on safety grounds after inspectors found cracks in the main beam.

Traffic will be restricted to the hard shoulder during emergency repairs, which are expected to last six to eight weeks. The bridge carries 36,500 vehicles a day, including 15,500 heavy goods vehicles.

On the first day of the works, September 17, a 12km tailback built up behind the bridge, adding an hour to the journey.

Transport en Logistiek Nederland (TLN), which represents the sector, surveyed its members on the impact of the closure and found that they expect journeys to take an extra 15 to 60 minutes.

Every 30-minute delay costs €600,000 when projected across an entire day’s traffic, TLN calculated.

“The longer the disruption lasts, the faster the damage adds up,” said TLN chair Elisabeth Post. “Especially if the old bridge eventually has to be removed entirely, which will reduce capacity further.”

The road and rail bridges were last renovated in 2021, ahead of plans to replace them entirely after 2030.

The state of infrastructure in the Netherlands is becoming a growing problem. The Merwedebrug, which takes traffic on the A27, was closed to lorries and coaches in July, at a cost of €1.5 million a day, while the A28 at Nijkerk was shut for 48 hours at the start of September after inspectors found sand and gravel holding up the base supports had been eroded.

The government announced an extra investment of €1.5 billion in next year’s budget to spend on maintaining roads, railways and waterways, but the full cost of the maintenance backlog is estimate to run into the tens of millions.

item.title: Gelderland to impose nitrogen limits on farms despite BBB split
item.description:
Gelderland to impose nitrogen limits on farms despite BBB split

September 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Gelderland has become the first province to restrict farming in “buffer zones” around nature reserves to bring down nitrogen compound emissions.

The provincial assembly voted to draw a 500-metre cordon around the Veluwe and three other vulnerable areas, in anticipation of nationwide restrictions that the government is drawing up.

New livestock farms and extensions to existing ones will be banned within the buffer zones from this year.

Other limitations will be phased in over the next 10 years, including a ban on synthetic fertiliser, restrictions on gas consumption and an obligation to make cattle sheds more energy efficient.

The plans have divided the parties in the agricultural province, which has the highest levels of ammonia pollution in the Netherlands.

They were drawn up by Ans Mol, executive member for the farmers’ party BBB, who said that doing nothing would mean “very big risks” for the sector. But seven of the BBB’s 12 assembly members voted against the plan.

Farmers’ protests

Coalition partners VVD, CDA, ChristenUnie and the SGP all backed the measures, which were also supported by the opposition parties GroenLinks, PvdA and D66.

Farmers picketed the provincial assembly building in Arnhem at the weekend to protest against nitrogen restrictions, arguing that they were not supported by evidence and deprived farmers of a future.

The provincial plans have been announced while the government in The Hague is still drawing up its own schedule of measures to bring down nitrogen pollution so that major housebuilding and infrastructure projects can go ahead.

Chris Backes, professor of environmental law at Utrecht University, has warned that some provinces will have to bring in their own measures to prevent the government using the “emergency brake” of a 5% to 10% reduction in heads of cattle.

Farmers are also facing legal action from environmental campaign groups such as Mobilisation for the Environment (MOB), which has petitioned regional courts to cancel the licences for 130 farm businesses.

All construction projects have to obtain a nature permit which shows they comply with environmental regulations, including European limits on nitrogen compound emissions around Natura-2000 conservation areas.

item.title: Jetten warns Trump of “jeopardising” relations over ICC
item.description:
Jetten warns Trump of “jeopardising” relations over ICC

September 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten has said the Dutch are pulling out all of the diplomatic stops to prevent further sanctions against the International Criminal Court in The Hague, warning American president Donald Trump against further escalations.

”My message to President Trump is very clear: don’t do it. Do not further jeopardise the relationship between Europe and the US by imposing new sanctions on the ICC,” Jetten told journalists in New York.

The prime minister is set to address the United Nations later today.

The Wall Street Journal, Reuters and the Associated Press have all reported in recent days that the United States is planning to escalate its fight with the ICC and sanction the institution as a whole as part of its campaign to dismantle the court “brick by brick”.

The White House has already sanctioned 13 staff members, including court president, Japanese Judge Tomoko Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

As the court’s host state, the Netherlands is obliged to provide assistance such as cooperation with security, facilitating visas and transporting defendants and witnesses.

A number of opposition parties in the Netherlands feel the government is not doing enough to protect the institution. MP Kati Piri of Pro told public broadcaster NOS that the cabinet has adopted a “super weak” stance so far.

In a letter to parliament earlier this month, foreign affairs minister Tom Berendsen said the Dutch had been regularly meeting with the court and other countries to discuss the situation, writing that “Dutch efforts have contributed to the court’s ability … to continue the vast majority of its operations unimpeded thus far.”

item.title: House price growth slows to 3.3%, transactions fall
item.description:
House price growth slows to 3.3%, transactions fall

September 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

House prices increased by 3.3% in August, continuing a slowdown that began at the start of 2025.

The latest monthly update by the statistics agency CBS showed prices fell by 0.1% from July to August. The number of transactions was also down by 2.9% compared to a year ago.

House price growth peaked at 11.5% in January 2025 as the market recovered from a brief slump in 2023, but since then the rate has decline steadily.

The average price paid for a house, excluding newbuild properties, increased to €503,523, having passed the half-million mark in July. On average prices are now 17.8% higher than the last peak in July 2022.

item.description:
Zeeland warns of oil pollution on beaches

September 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Oil has washed up on several beaches across Zeeland, and the province has warned that swimmers should stay out of the water where the substance has been found.

The first oil was found at the weekend, on the beach in the village of Westkapelle. Over the last few days, deposits have been found in multiple places along the coast.

The province warns people not to touch the oil and advises swimmers to stay out of the water near where oil has been found.

Oil can cause adverse skin reactions and the province advises that if you or your pets come into contact with it to wash thoroughly with soap and water.

It is unclear where the oil originated from. According to the province, the substance is mostly heavy fuel oil.

item.title: Around 70 people in Netherlands branded “security threat”
item.description:
Around 70 people in Netherlands branded “security threat”

September 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch immigration ministry has labelled around 70 people a threat to national security in the past 10 years, revoking residency permits and, in the case of dual nationals, their passports.

The figures from IND were uncovered in an investigation by Nieuwsuur.

Most of those have been convicted of terrorism-related offences, the news programme found. Three of the men involved in planning an attack in Arnhem were among those given the designation.

Not everybody on the list is a terrorist. A Russian national who is suspected of stealing secrets from Dutch chip machinery makers ASML was also labelled a threat.

The justice ministry would not confirm how many people on the list were still in custody.

Dual nationals or foreigners who are classed as a threat to national security are deported and banned from re-entering the Netherlands. However, not everyone has actually left the country.

In May, the justice ministry acknowledge that it has not been possible to remove everyone. Many countries will not take their nationals back or revoke their travel documents.

item.title: Groningen and Drenthe to host 2034 world cycling championships
item.description:
Groningen and Drenthe to host 2034 world cycling championships

September 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The world road cycling championships are returning to the Netherlands for the first time in more than 20 years after Groningen and Drenthe won the contest to stage the 2034 edition.

The two northern provinces had originally bid for the championships in 2032, but the international cycling union UCI awarded that year’s event to Pune, the first time it will be held in India.

“It’s brilliant that this is happening, it’s really a dream,” said Bauke Mollema, Groningen-born Tour de France veteran who acted as ambassador for the Dutch bid. “As a northerner, I learned to cycle on the roads of Groningen and Drenthe.”

The Netherlands has hosted the road race championships eight times before, most recently in Valkenburg in 2012, when Marianne Vos won her second world title.

The exact dates and the route for 2034 still have to be worked out, but the Vamberg or “Col du Vam” – a 63 metre-high artificial hill made of piled-up domestic rubbish from the Randstad – is certain to feature prominently. The hill is the only opportunity for climbing in the otherwise pancake-flat provinces.

The time trials are expected to start and finish at the TT circuit in Assen, while the organisers have promised the routes will pass through every municipality in the region.

The decision was announced by the UCI in Montreal, where this year’s championships are being held. One of the selling points of the Dutch bid was that the paralympic championships will be integrated into the main event.

“A paracycling event suits Drenthe brilliantly,” said organiser Thijs Rondhuis. “We held the world paracycling championships in Emmen in 2019. It’s about inclusion and everyone being able to take part.”

The bid has been underwritten with €20 million from Ny Begun, a fund set up to rebuild Groningen and northern Drenthe following the earthquakes caused by gas drilling.

item.title: “Facade politics” is making far-right ideas acceptable: AIVD
item.description:
“Facade politics” is making far-right ideas acceptable: AIVD

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Far-right organisations are using euphemistic terms such as “remigration” to establish racist and discriminatory ideas in mainstream debate, the Dutch security services have warned.

The intelligence agency AIVD and the national counter-terrorism co-ordinator said “façade politics” was designed to mask extremist ideas by expressing them in more palatable language.

Groups such as White Lives Matter, the Active Club Dietsland and the Greater Netherlands Student Union (GNSV) had emerged in the last 10 years under the banner of “identitarian resistance”, itself a euphemism for white supremacism.

“In reality many identitarians are convinced of ‘white superiority’ and show an aversion to other cultures and religions, as well as white people who think differently such as feminists and LGBTI+ people,” the agencies said.

Far-right groups are also infiltrating demonstrations against asylum seeker centres, organising international conferences and influencing political parties.

The right-wing parties JA21, Forum voor Democratie, Geert Wilders’ PVV and the the BoerBurgerBeweging took 30% of the vote between them in last October’s general election. All used the term “remigration” in their election manifestos.

Weekend riots

The report was published after a weekend in which 300 people gathered for an anti-immigration protest in The Hague organised by a group calling itself Wij Zijn Het Volk (“We are the people”).

Protesters made Nazi salutes, chanted anti-Semitic slogans and carried banners with messages such as “blanke mannen vooraan” (white men first).

The demonstration was cancelled after rioters clashed with police who ordered them to remove their face masks. Altogether 24 people were arrested. It was the second year in a row that an anti-immigration demonstration on the city’s Malieveld triggered violent confrontations with police.

The AIVD estimates that “several hundred Dutch people” are involved in right-wing terrorist activity and there is a real chance that some will resort to actual violence.

But they also said the groups were at undermining the democratic system “by stealth”, using social media platforms such as TikTok and X to spread extremist ideas.

“The effect in the long term can be greater than a terrorist attack,” the report said.

item.title: Dutch to return to Eurovision Song Contest in 2027 after boycott
item.description:
Dutch to return to Eurovision Song Contest in 2027 after boycott

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands will return to Eurovision in 2027, after pulling out this year over the participation of Israel.

Dutch public broadcaster NPO has taken over the reins after broadcaster AVROTROS announced earlier this year the country would not send a participant.

“The Song Contest was originally founded to bring people in Europe together. to bring together after the Second World War. We are seeking that connection again now,” Jet de Ranitz, of NPO’s executive board, said in a statement.

The Netherlands was one of five countries that refused to enter last year’s competition in response to the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, although the contest in Austria was still shown on Dutch TV by public broadcaster NPO. Ireland has said it will stay away again in 2027, with Spain likely to follow suit.

The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) has since changed its rules to ban winning countries from hosting the following year’s event if they are involved in a “sensitive geopolitical situation” that affects the “security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region”.

item.title: Freelancing in the Netherlands? First get your tax sorted!
item.description:
Partner content

Freelancing in the Netherlands? First get your tax sorted!

September 23, 2026

Setting up your own business or going it alone as a freelancer takes a lot of time and energy, and it is easy to forget some of the things you need to do. For example, if you are considering becoming a ZZP’er, how can you make sure you keep on the right side of the taxman?

Dealing with BTW

One of the first bits of paperwork you will be confronted with if you go into business in the Netherlands is dealing with BTW — omzetbelasting, or value added tax. “What people often forget is that they do have to submit their VAT return every three months even if they have only just started in business,” says Andra Radu, from Taxmo, an online bookkeeping and tax platform for freelancers, which largely focuses on helping internationals.

“Your first VAT deadline can arrive sooner than you expect. Starting a business doesn’t necessarily mean you have three months before you need to think about VAT. Depending on when you register, the VAT quarter may already be underway. And even if you haven’t made much money yet, you may still have a return to submit.”

Using a smart bookkeeping software, like that developed by Taxmo, means you can produce and send your invoices, keep a record of suppliers and upload the invoices they have sent you, calculate your personal expenses, and deal with your VAT and your income tax on one all-encompassing platform. You don’t even have to fill in the tax office’s own forms because Taxmo does it for you.

Understanding tax terminology

For many internationals, the difficult part isn’t running the business itself, it’s understanding the language and administration around it. You must file a VAT return if you are registered as an entrepreneur with the tax office (and have been assigned a VAT number starting with NL), if you are a ZZP’er — or freelancer — or if you are running a VOF, BV, or eenmanszaak (partnership, limited company, or sole proprietorship).

The jargon can seem incomprehensible and Dutch tax terms, unfamiliar deadlines and different rules for different types of clients can make a relatively simple freelance business feel much more complicated than it actually is.

Tax rules for freelancers

One rule freelancers may not be aware of, for example, is the KOR — yes, more jargon — the small business ruling, which, simply put, means that if you book annual turnover of less than €20,000 a year, you may be able to avoid dealing with VAT altogether.

Qualifying for the KOR doesn’t automatically mean it’s the best choice for your business. If you have significant business expenses, being unable to reclaim VAT on them can make a difference. It’s also worth thinking about how quickly you expect your business to grow rather than looking only at your turnover today.

“Business expenses are another area where new freelancers can easily get confused,” says Andra. “Keeping track of invoices, receipts and expenses from the beginning makes life much easier when it’s time to file, particularly when you’re still learning which costs actually count.”

Cross-border VAT

As an international freelancer, you may well have clients in other countries, and that’s something you’ll need to sort out too when keeping on top of your taxes. “This is particularly relevant for internationals, who often continue working with clients outside the Netherlands after setting up here,” Andra points out.

“You might have a Dutch client, an EU client and a US or UK client in your first few months of freelancing. How you handle VAT can depend on where the client is based, whether they’re a business or consumer and what you’re selling, so it isn’t always as simple as adding 21% to an invoice.”

File your tax returns yourself

Of course, smart software cannot solve all problems. There will always be situations where professional advice is useful, particularly as a business becomes more complex. But freelancers with relatively straightforward businesses don’t necessarily need to outsource every VAT return or routine piece of administration.

“Becoming a ZZP’er does not mean you need to understand every part of the Dutch tax system yourself or hire an expensive accountant for every filing,” says Andra. “Our platform has been designed specifically for the Dutch situation, to make sure you can do as much as you can yourself. We are all Dutch taxpayers even if we don’t speak the local language, or at any rate not much. Paying tax is not something you can avoid, but you can make it as easy as possible.”

Find out here how Taxmo helps freelancers handle bookkeeping, VAT and income tax in the Netherlands, without having to become Dutch tax experts themselves.
